title: Acute arrhythmia
banner: DRAFT, NOT clinically reviewed. Fictional scenario specification; never imported, published or shown to learners.
learning_objectives: Go to the patient when the monitor shows a new abnormal rhythm and assess for signs of reduced cardiac output.
Know that fast wide rhythms and certain other rhythms need emergency help, and call for it.
Prepare equipment and support the team; leave rhythm treatment (medicines, cardioversion, defibrillation) to trained staff acting under protocol.
Look for reversible causes, and document and hand over the rhythm.

setting: A fictional adult on telemetry in a fictional intensive care unit.

steps.info: During cardiac monitoring, a new fast, wide-complex rhythm appears. The awake patient reports dizziness and chest discomfort, and pressure is lower than before. The displayed rhythm alone does not establish perfusion or the required treatment.
steps.prompt: What takes priority when a new wide-complex rhythm is accompanied by symptoms?

options.text: Assess the patient immediately: pulse, pressure, skin, consciousness, chest pain and breathing. Call emergency help; check electrodes without delaying care.
options.feedback: When the ECG shows a new abnormal finding the nurse immediately assesses the client for signs of decreased cardiac output, and the nurse must know which rhythms need emergency assistance, including ventricular tachycardia.
options.consequence: Immediate patient and pulse assessment may identify haemodynamic instability and support timely emergency rhythm evaluation.

options.text: Print the rhythm strip and place it with the observations in the notes, then repeat the rhythm and pressure readings in a few minutes before deciding whether to call for urgent help.
options.feedback: A rhythm strip is useful, but delaying patient assessment and urgent help in a symptomatic wide-complex tachyarrhythmia is unsafe.
options.consequence: Printing a strip before assessing the patient could delay recognition of circulatory compromise.

options.text: Silence the alarm, review the monitor trend and continue routine observation because the patient is still awake and can describe the discomfort; report it if responsiveness worsens.
options.feedback: Some rhythms are tolerated only briefly before the patient loses consciousness; an awake patient does not make the rhythm safe.
options.consequence: Being awake could falsely reassure staff while the rhythm and perfusion worsen.

steps.info: At the next shared checkpoint, the wide-complex rhythm continues, pressure is falling and confusion is increasing. A pulse is still present. The emergency team has arrived and must determine the rhythm-specific treatment.
steps.prompt: How should the nurse support treatment of this unstable rhythm while remaining prepared for loss of pulse?

options.text: Bring emergency equipment and defibrillator, secure IV access, monitor and document. Support authorised rhythm-specific care; prepare for CPR if arrest occurs.
options.feedback: An unstable tachyarrhythmia with a pulse needs urgent rhythm-specific treatment by authorised trained staff; synchronised cardioversion is preferred for many unstable tachyarrhythmias, but rhythm and synchronisation feasibility matter. If cardiac arrest occurs, start CPR and follow the shockable versus non-shockable arrest pathway. Not every pulseless rhythm requires a shock. The 2025 RCUK adult ALS guidance favors electrical cardioversion for unstable tachyarrhythmia with life-threatening features. When a synchronized shock is indicated, the trained operator verifies synchronization; preparation for sedation or anesthesia in a conscious patient must not create avoidable delay in emergency care. Do not apply this to physiological sinus tachycardia. In particular, AHA 2025 recommends synchronized cardioversion for unstable wide-complex tachycardia when appropriate to the rhythm and advises against adenosine in unstable, irregular or polymorphic wide-complex rhythms. Polymorphic VT requires a different shock strategy; confirm the rhythm with the trained team.
options.consequence: Coordinated emergency preparation and continuous reassessment may support timely authorized treatment and recognition of cardiac arrest if it occurs.

options.text: Prepare the defibrillator and deliver a shock independently before the trained team has assessed the rhythm and selected the appropriate electrical treatment, to avoid further delay.
options.feedback: Do not deliver an unassessed or unauthorised shock. The team must determine the rhythm, pulse and appropriate synchronisation or defibrillation pathway; not all rhythms with a pulse have the same treatment.
options.consequence: An unassessed or unauthorized shock could use an inappropriate mode or cause avoidable harm.

options.text: Remain beside the monitor, record the rhythm and pressure for the emergency team, and leave all bedside assessment, access preparation and resuscitation readiness to the responding clinicians.
options.feedback: Watching the monitor alone is insufficient during deteriorating perfusion. Remain with the patient, assist the emergency team and prepare time-critical care.
options.consequence: Monitor-only observation could delay equipment preparation and recognition of changing patient perfusion.

steps.info: At the final shared checkpoint, the rhythm has slowed and pressure is improving after team-directed treatment. The patient is tired but comfortable. A recent potassium result is available and further cause assessment and post-treatment monitoring are needed.
steps.prompt: Which follow-up best identifies reversible contributors and early recurrence after rhythm treatment?

observations.label: Follow-up
observations.value: Review reversible contributors and treatment response

options.text: Report electrolyte results and possible causes; continuously monitor pressure and rhythm after treatment. Time-stamp rhythm strips and give SBAR handover.
options.feedback: Reversible causes of dangerous rhythms include low or high potassium, hypoxia and low blood volume; antidysrhythmic medicines such as amiodarone can cause hypotension, a slow heart rate and heart block, so these are monitored after treatment.
options.consequence: Continued monitoring and communication of electrolyte and rhythm trends may reveal recurrence or treatment-related adverse effects.

options.text: Record the improved rhythm and blood pressure, then widen the alarm limits to prevent repeated alerts overnight, leaving the next review of the limits for the morning team.
options.feedback: Limits and alarms are set by order or protocol; widening them removes the warning the patient needs.
options.consequence: Widening alarm limits could conceal another clinically important rhythm change.

options.text: Document the rhythm conversion and allow the patient to rest by removing the monitoring electrodes; resume continuous monitoring only if the patient reports recurring symptoms.
options.feedback: Monitoring continues after a dangerous rhythm because it can recur.
options.consequence: Removing monitoring could delay recognition of recurrent arrhythmia or post-treatment instability.

learning_points: A new abnormal rhythm needs immediate assessment of the patient for signs of reduced cardiac output, and a call for help when the rhythm or the patient's condition is dangerous.
Fast wide rhythms and several other rhythms can lead quickly to loss of consciousness or cardiac arrest.
Support urgent rhythm-specific care by trained and authorised staff. If cardiac arrest occurs, begin CPR and follow the appropriate shockable or non-shockable rhythm pathway.
Think about reversible causes such as electrolytes and oxygenation, keep monitoring after treatment and hand over with SBAR.

For an unstable abnormal tachyarrhythmia with a pulse, prepare the trained-team cardioversion pathway, including synchronization and appropriate sedation assessment; if the pulse is lost, switch to the arrest pathway.
